claim: For pairwise coprime integers m_1,...,m_k and M_i equal to the product of all m_j with j≠i, one has gcd(m_i,M_i)=1 for every i.
evidence: If gcd(r,s)=gcd(r,t)=1, choose integers A,B,C,D with Ar+Bs=1 and Cr+Dt=1. Multiplication yields 1=r(ACr+ADt+BCs)+BDst, hence gcd(r,st)=1. Iterating this identity over the factors m_j (j≠i), each coprime to m_i, proves gcd(m_i,M_i)=1. claim: If pairwise coprime integers m_1,...,m_k each divide an integer z, then their product M divides z.
evidence: First, if gcd(r,s)=1 and r|z and s|z, write z=rq and choose A,B with Ar+Bs=1. Multiplying by q gives q=Az+Bsq. Both terms on the right are divisible by s, so s|q and rs|z. Induct on the number of moduli: the product of the first h moduli is coprime to m_{h+1} by the preceding elementary product-coprimality argument, so the two-factor result extends divisibility by the partial product to divisibility by the next partial product.
